x: Panel discussion: Securing AI-Driven Organizations — Governance, Trust and Responsible Innovation
AI governance starts with knowing its tools, data and permissions

Muscat — Panelists at CyberX Oman 2026 discussed the challenges of adopting AI inside organizations, with a focus on protecting data, controlling what AI agents are allowed to do, and defining who is accountable for decisions these technologies support.

A recurring idea was that the speed of adoption can outpace an organization's ability to set clear rules for use. The fix starts with knowing which tools are actually in use, what data they reach, and what permissions they hold — before scaling them up.
Panelists
Ramya Sankari Karthick: moderator, and Head of IT at Zawawi Powertech Engineering LLC.
Dr. Haitham Al Hajri: Head of Cybersecurity and Information Security at Oman Housing Bank.
Ali Al-Lawati: Founder and CTO of QPay Oman.
Vivek Baniya: Information Security Officer at Liva Insurance Oman.
Mohammed Tajuddin: Product Manager for Network, Content and Data Security at Securado.

Ramya opened the session by asking the audience about the gap between AI tools being officially approved and actually being used inside organizations — putting the gap between adoption and governance at the center of the discussion.
Know the real usage first
The session looked at how AI is embedded in cloud services and business applications, including tools employees may use without official approval.

The discussion covered four layers of discovery: device and network logs; applications and APIs connected to external models; the models and the environments hosting them; and AI agents with their permissions, tools and memory.
The goal is a clear picture of how users, agents, models and data relate to each other, helping the organization pinpoint where risk comes from and put the right controls in place.
Governance before scale

Dr. Haitham Al Hajri warned against adopting AI tools under organizational pressure without defining the need for them. He raised questions that should come before any purchase or rollout: what is the tool for? Which department will use it? What data will it process? And what outcome is expected?
He stressed the importance of a clear acceptable-use policy, with an example of using AI in security operations centers to sift through large volumes of logs and flag what deserves investigation.
Minimize data and test systems

Ali Al-Lawati shared lessons from digital finance, focusing on minimizing the data used in credit scoring, limiting tools' access to personally identifiable information, and controlling agents' permissions and instructions.

He also covered testing systems in isolated environments before running them in production, and pointed to requirements for hosting data inside Oman in the context of his platform's operations and regulatory oversight.
Speed with human oversight
Vivek Baniya shared an example of using a language model to analyze more than 17,000 logs in about an hour and a half, helping identify when an attack began and which systems it affected.
He focused on benefiting from that speed while verifying the results and keeping high-risk decisions under the oversight of specialists and those with the authority to make them.
Controlling AI agents' permissions
The discussion addressed how AI agents differ from traditional applications: some can use tools, access data and take actions inside systems.
Proposed controls included granting the least privilege needed, defining the allowed tools, separating read, write and delete permissions, and monitoring agents' behavior at runtime.
The panel also discussed the risk of granting AI tools broad administrative permissions at install time without tying those permissions to a specific task.
Accountability and local readiness
Speakers stressed that accountability stays with the organization and its leadership, even when AI tools are used to support decisions.

On local readiness, Dr. Haitham Al Hajri said organizations still need to mature their privacy and accountability practices around these technologies, and that international frameworks need to be adapted to Omani legislation and needs.
The discussion touched on the Personal Data Protection Law, awareness materials and the national language model as elements in the panelists' assessment of readiness.
Examples from the session
Analyzing more than 17,000 logs in about an hour and a half, in the incident-response case presented by Vivek Baniya.
An example from Ali Al-Lawati of a possible fraud pattern: four transactions within three minutes for different amounts, warranting a context-based review.
An experience with an e-KYC provider involving data being retained for 90 days after the service ended, and a request for proof of deletion.
Audience questions

Audience questions covered securing AI agents, choosing platforms, and handling requests from different departments. The answers highlighted data classification, clear ownership, and the option of a committee or internal body to oversee AI use.

Risks of intellectual property leaking through coding tools, and of data deletion when switching providers, were also raised. Solutions discussed included organization-controlled development environments, contractual commitments, encryption, and exit clauses with proof of deletion.
On national policy, one panelist referred to an upcoming draft policy, without enough detail to identify the issuing body or release date.
Recommendations from the discussion
Inventory AI tools, both approved and used without official approval.
Define the purpose, data and beneficiary before adoption.
Set an acceptable-use policy and tie access to data classification.
Give agents the least privilege needed and monitor them at runtime.
Keep high-risk decisions under human oversight.
Assign an internal owner for AI governance.
Include data protection, exit and proof-of-deletion terms in contracts.
Train employees and apply data loss prevention controls.
The discussion concluded that safe adoption requires knowing real usage, controlling access to data and defining accountability, with ongoing review of risks and outcomes.
